classification.difficultyReason: Select integer roots, remove common factors where present, and repeatedly divide to leave one quadratic factor.

content.prompt: Factorise each polynomial as a product of linear factors and one quadratic factor.

answer.worked:
$$P(1)=1+2+2-5=0$$
Thus $x-1$ is a factor. Long division gives
$$\frac{P(x)}{x-1}=x^2+3x+5.$$
Hence
$$P(x)=(x-1)(x^2+3x+5).$$
The quadratic has discriminant $3^2-4(1)(5)=-11<0$, so it has no further linear factors.

$$\begin{align*}P(-1)&=-1+4-4+3=2\ne0\\P(-3)&=-27+36-12+3=0\end{align*}$$
Thus $x+3$ is a factor. Long division gives
$$\frac{P(x)}{x+3}=x^2+x+1.$$
Hence
$$P(x)=(x+3)(x^2+x+1).$$
The quadratic has discriminant $1^2-4(1)(1)=-3<0$, so it has no further linear factors.

answer.short:
$x^2(x-2)(x^2+6x-3)$

Take out $x^2$, then use the factor theorem and long division.
answer.worked:
$$P(x)=x^2(x^3+4x^2-15x+6).$$
Let $Q(x)=x^3+4x^2-15x+6$.
$$\begin{align*}Q(1)&=1+4-15+6=-4\ne0\\Q(-1)&=-1+4+15+6=24\ne0\\Q(2)&=8+16-30+6=0\end{align*}$$
Thus $x-2$ is a factor of $Q(x)$. Long division gives
$$\frac{Q(x)}{x-2}=x^2+6x-3.$$
Hence
$$P(x)=x^2(x-2)(x^2+6x-3).$$
The quadratic has no integer roots, so it has no further linear factors with integer coefficients.

answer.short:
$(x-2)(x+3)(x^2+3x+1)$

Apply the factor theorem and long division twice.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}P(1)&=1+4-2-17-6=-20\ne0\\P(-1)&=1-4-2+17-6=6\ne0\\P(2)&=16+32-8-34-6=0\end{align*}$$
Thus $x-2$ is a factor. Long division gives
$$P(x)=(x-2)(x^3+6x^2+10x+3).$$
Let $Q(x)=x^3+6x^2+10x+3$.
$$\begin{align*}Q(-1)&=-1+6-10+3=-2\ne0\\Q(-3)&=-27+54-30+3=0\end{align*}$$
Long division by $x+3$ gives
$$Q(x)=(x+3)(x^2+3x+1).$$
Hence
$$P(x)=(x-2)(x+3)(x^2+3x+1).$$
The quadratic has no integer roots, so it has no further linear factors with integer coefficients.
